name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
description: The CIFAR-10 dataset consists of 60,000 32x32 colour images across 10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck), with 6,000 images per class. The CIFAR-100 dataset contains 600 images in each of 100 non-overlapping classes organized into 20 superclasses of 5 classes each. Both datasets are labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset collected by groups at MIT and NYU. The datasets were created to enable object recognition experiments using reliable class labels derived from human labeling of web-scraped images.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. Technical Report.
rai:dataCollection: The underlying tiny images dataset was assembled by colleagues at MIT and NYU by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results per search term. The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 labeled subsets were created by paying students to label images from this dataset, filtering out mislabeled images based on defined criteria.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of 80 million colour images downscaled to 32x32 pixels collected from the web via search engines (Google, Flickr, Altavista) using every non-abstract English noun in WordNet as search terms, keeping roughly the first 3000 results per search term. The search term used to find an image provides a rough but unreliable label.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months (exact dates not specified). The CIFAR-100 dataset was described as only very recently completed at the time of writing (April 2009).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collecting images for each search term, perfect duplicates were removed, as were images in which an excessively large portion of pixels were white (as they tended to be synthetic figures). For the labeled subsets, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs. The dataset was divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. For model training, a ZCA whitening transformation was applied to decorrelate pixel values. Additionally, the 1000 least-significant directions of variance (smallest principal components) were deleted from the dataset to reduce high-frequency noise. For object classification experiments, both whitened and unwhitened versions of the data were used.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human labelers (paid students) were given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with hyponyms of the main search term (as defined by WordNet). Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to their assigned class based on the following criteria: (1) the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?'; (2) the image should be photo-realistic (line drawings rejected); (3) the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object; (4) the object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is clear. Labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour. All labels submitted by labelers were personally verified by the authors.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Every label submitted by the labelers was personally verified by the authors. The instruction sheet specified that false positives (incorrectly included images) are worse than false negatives (incorrectly excluded images), biasing labelers toward conservative inclusion.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Paid students (no further demographic details provided).
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The CIFAR-100 dataset includes a 'people' superclass with classes: baby, boy, girl, man, woman.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables object recognition research and the development of deep generative models that learn features resembling those found in the human visual cortex, potentially advancing computer vision and AI capabilities.
rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides only a rough and extremely unreliable label due to the nature of online image search technology. Images tend to exhibit symmetry about the vertical and horizontal axes, likely caused by the way people take photographs (making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object).
rai:dataLimitations: The original tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use directly for object recognition experiments. The labeled CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 subsets address this but cover only 10 and 100 classes respectively out of 79,000 search terms. All experiments reported were with CIFAR-10 as CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed at time of writing.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and testing object recognition models. The CIFAR-10 dataset (5000 training images and 1000 test images per class) is used for supervised classification experiments. The larger unlabeled tiny images dataset is used for unsupervised pre-training of deep generative models (RBMs/DBNs). CIFAR-100 classes can also be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10 classification.
